Week 56 Appendix: A Week That Held Its Ground

Executive power converted earlier gains into standing rule this week, while courts and Congress applied friction without reversing the underlying trend.

This was a high-pressure week centered on the politicization of state capacity: the federal workforce, the justice system, immigration enforcement, and election administration were all pushed in more openly partisan directions. The most consequential single move was the finalization of rules stripping civil-service protections from roughly 50,000 federal employees, which directly increases executive control over the bureaucracy and weakens whistleblower and merit safeguards. A second major theme was the fusion of immigration enforcement with exceptional, often legally dubious coercive power: detention expansion, prolonged custody despite court orders or valid status, reduced access to counsel and medical care, and aggressive operations that triggered both protests and repeated judicial intervention. Third, the week showed a sharp escalation in election restriction efforts through the SAVE America Act, North Carolina challenge rules, and threats to federalize elections. Running through all of this was evidence of retaliatory or politicized law enforcement and information control, especially DOJ monitoring of congressional review activity, suppression or distortion around the Epstein files, and executive manipulation of public memory and symbolic space.

Power and Authority

  1. The Office of Personnel Management issued a final rule removing civil service protections from about 50,000 federal employees: The rule increased presidential control over the federal workforce and weakened merit-based independence and whistleblower safeguards inside agencies. (2026-02-07)
  2. President Trump withheld Gateway tunnel funding and the administration appealed orders requiring its release: Using major infrastructure funds as leverage for personal or political aims tested limits on executive spending power and fair treatment of disfavored jurisdictions. (2026-02-09)
  3. The Department of Homeland Security expanded immigrant detention capacity through new facilities and warehouse conversion plans: The buildout sharply increased federal coercive capacity in immigration enforcement and deepened reliance on mass detention as a governing tool. (2026-02-13)
  4. The Department of Veterans Affairs ended its care agreement with ICE detainees and ICE stopped paying outside medical providers: The decisions used executive control over detention services in ways that reduced basic care for people in custody and weakened accountability for humane treatment. (2026-02-08)
  5. President Trump pardoned January 6 defendant Andrew Paul Johnson: The pardon used clemency power to reduce accountability for an attack tied to the disruption of democratic transfer of power. (2026-02-11)
  6. President Trump issued an executive order directing the military to buy coal-generated power and support coal plants: The order used executive and military purchasing power to favor a politically aligned industry and bypass normal policy tradeoffs on energy and public welfare. (2026-02-12)
  7. Governor Mikie Sherrill signed an order limiting immigration agents’ access to non-public state property without a judicial warrant: The order used state executive power to check federal immigration operations and protect due process on state-controlled property. (2026-02-12) [single source]
  8. The Trump administration and EPA Administrator Lee Zeldin rescinded the greenhouse-gas endangerment finding and moved to end EPA greenhouse-gas regulation: The rollback used executive authority to strip a core legal basis for climate regulation, reducing public-health protections and narrowing future accountability. (2026-02-12)
  9. The Trump administration rescinded congressionally authorized research grants and required federally funded research to align with its ideology: The move used spending power to pressure universities and researchers, weakening academic independence and narrowing the range of protected inquiry. (2026-02-10) [single source]
  10. The Trump administration removed the Pride flag from the Stonewall national monument under a new flag-display policy: The action used federal control of public space to limit symbolic recognition of a marginalized community and shape official memory. (2026-02-10) [single source]
  11. The Trump administration canceled federal support for offshore wind ports and issued emergency orders to keep coal plants open: The actions used executive energy powers to favor fossil fuels over cleaner alternatives, shifting public resources and regulatory priorities by fiat. (2026-02-10) [single source]
  12. The Department of Homeland Security announced that the Department of Homeland Security would shut down without new funding: The looming shutdown showed how executive operations in a major security department were exposed to brinkmanship over immigration power and funding. (2026-02-12)
  13. Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem announced the termination of Temporary Protected Status for Yemen: Ending TPS exposed thousands of people to deportation and showed executive control over legal status as a direct tool shaping rights and security. (2026-02-13) [single source]
  14. The FDA refused to consider Moderna’s mRNA flu-shot application: The refusal affected public-health governance by narrowing a pathway for vaccine review and raising concerns about politicized decision-making in federal health power. (2026-02-13)
  15. The EPA reduced enforcement of major environmental laws against polluters: A sharp drop in enforcement weakened deterrence and showed executive discretion being used to ease accountability for regulated industries. (2026-02-13)
